transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-03
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Diaz (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Verdigris VP Eng), Anika Shah (Verdigris MLOps), Peter Goldman (Verdigris CISO)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Verdigris is evaluating Redwood for a Q3 pilot. Key constraints: strict cost cap (~$30k/mo for pilot), latency P95 target ~200ms for chat surfaces, SOC2 and VPC requirement, and preference for predictable billing. They want to understand per-token maths, batching/caching levers, and whether Dedicated or Private is needed for compliance and cost predictability. Next steps: pricing spreadsheet, perf scenarios, and sample traffic benchmark session.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching impact, KV/prefix caching, dedicated vs hosted predictability, VPC/private deployment constraints, KMS and audit logs, pilot scope and success metrics.

Action Items (automated): see action_items field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samantha from Redwood — AE on the account. Quick intros?
[00:12] Marcus: Marcus Li, VP Eng, Verdigris. We run the customer support assistant and an ops summarization service.
[00:18] Anika: Hi, Anika, lead MLOps — I'll share the usage numbers after this.
[00:23] Peter: Peter, CISO — I'll focus on security, network, compliance.
[00:30] Ravi: Ravi Patel, solutions engineer at Redwood — I'll walk through perf and batching.

[01:02] Samantha: Cool. The goal today is cost/unit economics — get a realistic sense of what hosted looks like, when Dedicated makes sense, and what tradeoffs you get with caching and batching. Also, capture any compliance needs. Marcus, can you give the volume/context?
[01:20] Marcus: Yeah. For the assistant we expect peak 120 RPS, average 40 RPS. Most sessions are short — median length about 75 tokens per request but tail goes to 1.2k tokens for longer threads. Monthly tokens about 400M right now, but that could double in 6 months. Budget for a pilot is tight, roughly $25–35k per month, hence why the per-token sensitivity matters.
[01:50] Samantha: Got it. And your latency targets?
[01:55] Marcus: For the chat UI, p95 should be under 200ms ideally, p99 under 350ms. For longer summarization jobs we can accept longer latency.
[02:10] Ravi: Quick qualifier — are you comfortable with a hosted cloud endpoint (Redwood hosted) or do you need a VPC/private deployment from day one?
[02:20] Anika: Security-wise, we prefer VPC for production due to data residency and network egress policies, but for pilot we might accept hosted if logs and encryption are OK. We need SOC2 evidence and KMS integration.
[02:36] Peter: Also SSO / SAML for access to console and audit logs; we need per-request auditability.

[03:00] Samantha: That aligns with typical customers — many do hosted pilot then Dedicated/VPC for prod. There is a cost delta: hosted is generally usage-based per-token; Dedicated is reserved capacity with predictable throughput and monthly commitment. We'll walk through the numbers.
[03:20] Marcus: Can you give a concrete per-token example? The marketing numbers are fuzzy.
[03:28] Samantha: Sure. Rough baseline: hosted model family X (open model equivalent) is listed at $0.0009 per input token and $0.0020 per output token — ballpark. But effective unit price can drop with batching and prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts. For Dedicated, you'll buy reserved GPU capacity — depending on model size, that might be say $Xk per GPU per month, but your per-token drops significantly since amortized cost plus higher throughput and you avoid per-token multipliers.
[04:05] Ravi: To make that real, if your median seq is 75 tokens and you have good prefix reuse we can often cache the KV for conversational histories and avoid re-computing early layers, which reduces time per token and effectively lowers cost by 15–40% depending on reuse.
[04:30] Marcus: How aggressive is that 15–40? What assumptions?
[04:34] Ravi: It's workload dependent — assumes 30–50% of calls share the same opening prompts or context (same user session). For pure one-off queries you get less benefit. Also quantization and batching efficiency play roles — with 4-bit quant we can increase throughput. But quant may impact quality slightly — evals catch that.
[04:58] Anika: We care about deterministic quality, can't have hallucination regressions. So quantization fine as long as evals pass.
[05:10] Samantha: We can run a small eval set with your prompts. We'll flag quality regressions. Our Optimize recommendations will say which quant profile to use for each endpoint.

[05:40] Marcus: Ok, back to math. If we do hosted and hit 400M tokens/mo, at $0.001 average that is $400k/month — way over our pilot. So the devil is in reuse and batching. What scenarios can bring that down to $30k?
[06:00] Ravi: There are levers: 1) batching to increase GPU utilization for short requests; 2) caching prefixes/KV; 3) routing to cheaper model variants for non-sensitive requests; 4) rate-limiting or token-slicing for higher-cost tails. In pilot we typically test two configs: baseline (no cache, minimal batching) and optimized (with KV cache, 50–100ms allowed queueing for batching) and compare.
[06:30] Marcus: Give me numbers — assume 400M tokens. If caching reduces token compute by 40%, and batching improves throughput such that effective per-token unit cost halves, what's the combined effect?
[06:44] Ravi: If caching reduces active compute tokens by 40% you go from 400M to 240M effective tokens. If batching halves per-token cost relative to baseline, you'd be at equivalently 120M token-cost. If baseline cost per token was $0.001, then that's ~$120k/mo. Still above $30k but closer. Add routing lower-cost model for 50% of calls and another 2x cost reduction for those, you can get under $40–50k in optimistic config.

[07:20] Anika: So pilot is important to measure our actual reuse and how many calls can go to cheaper models. We need Redwood to instrument token-level breakdowns.
[07:28] Samantha: Console shows token breakdowns per route/model with time series and cost attribution. We can give you an example dashboard.

[07:45] Peter: On Dedicated vs Hosted: is Dedicated always cheaper at scale? How do you price burst capacity?
[07:54] Samantha: Dedicated is priced as reserved GPU pools plus an optional burst overlay. The math: if you have sustained throughput and token volume, Dedicated amortizes the instance cost and can be 30–70% cheaper than hosted for heavy steady workloads. But Dedicated requires longer commitment and has provisioning lead-time. Bursting is available but billed differently.
[08:23] Marcus: Provisioning lead-time — how long?
[08:26] Ravi: Typically a few days to a couple weeks depending on scale and region. We have some fast lanes for pilots.

[08:40] Samantha: Also, with Dedicated you get isolation and easier egress control for compliance. Private (on-prem/VPC) gives max control but is the most ops-heavy and usually enterprise only.

[09:05] Marcus: On security: Peter needs to know whether we can integrate our KMS and keep keys on our side.
[09:12] Peter: Correct — and we need per-request audit logs, SIEM integration, and formal SOC2 artifacts. Also, data residency: some customers require EU-only storage.
[09:22] Samantha: We support customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated in VPC setups, and we have KMS integration options for hosted with Bring-Your-Own-Key in certain regions. We can share SOC2 Type II report and architecture diagram.
[09:40] Peter: Good. Also any model weights or prompts leave our network?
[09:44] Ravi: For hosted, inference runs on Redwood infra — data plane stays within chosen region but payloads are processed. For Dedicated/Private, you can isolate everything in your VPC or on-prem where we don't see plaintext model prompts if you configure encryption correctly. We'll include details in the security pack.

[10:10] Samantha: Back to cost levers: one more — routing by policy. You can route high-confidence / non-sensitive queries to cheaper models. We can do automatic fallback to a higher-quality model if the cheaper model fails a confidence threshold. That reduces avg cost while protecting quality.
[10:32] Marcus: How do we measure confidence? Is that a latency or token-based metric?
[10:36] Ravi: Confidence is application-specific; could be a separate classifier or a heuristic on token probabilities. We instrument fallbacks and would show the % of requests hitting baseline vs fallback.

[11:05] Anika: For the pilot we want to test three endpoints: chat (strict latency), background summarizer (throughput tolerant), and a small reranker. What would be a realistic pilot scope?
[11:17] Samantha: Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: integration, run benchmark window with sample traffic, analyze unit economics, then a recommendation (hosted vs Dedicated) and a small pilot SOW. For your budget we can scope a narrow pilot with 1–2 routes and constrained traffic to examine reuse and routing.

[11:50] Marcus: Timeline-wise, we want to decide by mid-May to budget for Q3. So the pilot needs to start in late April if possible.
[11:58] Samantha: We'll try to accommodate — next steps listed.

[12:25] Peter: On legal/procurement: do you have a standard data processing agreement and acceptable use? We have to review T&Cs and addendum.
[12:32] Samantha: Yes, we'll share standard DPA and we can work to add clauses for residency. Procurement lead time varies.

[13:00] Ravi: Quick dive into batching tradeoffs — we can accept a small queueing delay (e.g., 50–100ms) to aggregate requests into larger batches which increases GPU utilization. For chat UI that can be acceptable if p95 still meets 200ms. There's a balance: bigger batches = higher throughput but can increase p95 unless we partition by priority.
[13:32] Marcus: Can Redwood do multi-tiered queues? e.g., VIP traffic bypass batching, low-priority batched?
[13:38] Ravi: Yes, route-level SLOs and priority queues are supported. You can configure low-latency lanes and a batched lane for cheaper ops.

[14:00] Anika: About KV cache naming — we've seen docs mention KV cache and prefix cache, sometimes we call it K-V cash in notes. Clarify: that's the internal key-value cache for previous attention states, right?
[14:12] Ravi: Yeah, KV cache is the attention key/value cache saved per session. It lets the model avoid recomputing earlier tokens. If you persist and reuse those across requests, you save compute. We'll also talk about prefix caching where common opening prompts are cached.

[14:35] Marcus: What about cache eviction and storage costs? If we persist KV per user that's a lot of storage.
[14:41] Ravi: True — we give recommendations: keep 90% of active sessions resident with TTLs, evict old ones. Storage is modest relative to GPU but is a factor for huge user-bases. We'll show rough TB estimate from your session counts.

[15:05] Samantha: Any blockers on instrumentation? We need sample traffic and a small eval set for quality checks. That helps us decide quant profiles and routing rules.
[15:13] Anika: We'll export sample sessions and a 500-item eval prompt set.

[15:30] Marcus: Competitors — we looked at CloudVendorX who had a lower headline cost but opaque perf numbers; and EndpointServe who offer on-prem but with higher ops. Curious how Redwood compares latency-wise.
[15:44] Ravi: We can share benchmark numbers but they vary by model and seq lengths. Redwood's runtime focuses on continuous batching and attention optimizations which improve p95 for short sequences. We'll provide sample benchmarks for comparable models.

[16:10] Peter: For compliance, does Redwood support customer-managed KMS with HSM-backed keys in the region?
[16:17] Samantha: For Private and some Dedicated options yes, HSM-backed KMS is supported and we can sign an appropriate key-handling addendum. For hosted BYOK support is region-limited; we'll confirm which regions.

[16:45] Marcus: About pricing structure — you mentioned routing to cheaper models. Is that per-route configuration in Console? And can we set cost ceilings?
[16:55] Samantha: Yes, per-route model pinning and routing policies exist. You can set budgets and automated fallback if spend exceeds thresholds. Console exposes token burn and cost alerts.

[17:15] Anika: If we do Dedicated, how does autoscaling work? If traffic doubles, do GPUs spin up automatically?
[17:23] Ravi: There are autoscaling policies for Dedicated pools with buffer capacity and options for burst capacity against a managed overlay. But scaling has some provisioning time; for spikes you can use hosted fallback to absorb overflow.

[17:50] Marcus: That hosted fallback is interesting — so we could keep predictable base capacity in Dedicated and overflow to hosted at higher unit cost. That's a hybrid pattern right?
[17:58] Samantha: Exactly — hybrid routing for capacity spikes is common. It gives predictability for steady traffic and elasticity for spikes.

[18:20] Peter: What's the unit for billing? Tokens only? Any per-request or per-embedding minimums?
[18:26] Samantha: Billing is token-centric for text generation and embeddings units for embed calls. There are no per-request minimums but tiny requests are subject to batching overheads which influence effective cost. For Dedicated the model is capacity-based so billing is not per-token but reserved capacity plus any overages/burst.

[19:00] Marcus: Any tips to aggressively reduce burn without killing UX? We want to hit < $35k pilot if possible.
[19:06] Ravi: Tactics: 1) aggressive prefix caching for session-based chat; 2) route cheap model for informational queries; 3) limit model context window for low-value calls; 4) compress prompts; 5) use reranking to reduce generation length. We'll simulate these in the perf scenarios.

[19:40] Samantha: We'll put numbers in the pricing spreadsheet with optimistic/realistic/conservative columns.

[20:00] Anika: About audit logs — we need S3-like retention for 12 months and SIEM webhook. Can Redwood provide that?
[20:07] Samantha: Yes, we can stream audit logs to your S3 or SIEM with retention controls for Dedicated/VPC. Hosted can also export logs but may have region limitations. We'll document specifics.

[20:30] Marcus: Any red flags on latency if we enable heavier batching?
[20:34] Ravi: Depends on prioritization. If you route chat to low-queue lanes, p95 remains tight. For background jobs batching is fine. We can show p95 tradeoff curves during benchmark.

[21:00] Samantha: Quick recap before deeper perf numbers: 1) Pilot scope: 4–6 weeks for 2 routes; 2) Deliverables: pricing spreadsheet, perf scenarios, benchmark window; 3) Security docs and SOC2 pack; 4) Decision target mid-May. Is that right?
[21:20] Marcus: Yes.
[21:25] Peter: Yes, please include KMS and BYOK options and residency detail in the pack.

[21:40] Samantha: Great. We'll collect the sample traffic and eval set. Ravi, you'll own perf scenarios.
[21:47] Ravi: Yep. I'll draft three configs: baseline, batched+cache, and hybrid routing.

[22:05] Marcus: A note — we may have internal politics: product wants quality first, finance is pushing cost cap. So the pilot should show acceptable UX at a cost we can sell to finance.
[22:18] Samantha: Understood — we'll emphasize quality gating and present ruler thresholds.

[22:45] Anika: One more technical detail: we use a GRPC gateway internally and have websocket frontends. Any integration caveats?
[22:54] Ravi: We support REST/gRPC and streaming via websockets — we'll send an integration guide and sample client.

[23:15] Marcus: On metrics, we want to see token burn, per-route latency percentiles, % of requests hitting cheap model vs fallback, and cost per 1k requests.
[23:26] Samantha: All available in Console — we'll provide a sample dashboard.

[23:45] Peter: Any SLA thresholds for hosted? Or only Dedicated?
[23:50] Samantha: Hosted has standard availability SLAs; Dedicated gets stronger SLA, and Private is negotiable with enterprise support packs. We'll include SLA docs.

[24:15] Marcus: Regarding procurement, typical contract length for Dedicated?
[24:20] Samantha: Usually 6–12 month commitments. For pilot we use a short SOW and then convert.

[24:35] Anika: For the benchmark, do you want production traffic or synthetic?
[24:40] Ravi: Sample of production traffic is best to capture real session reuse; if not possible, a realistic synthetic mix with the same seq-length distribution is fine.

[25:00] Samantha: Ok let's move to some quick scenario math that Ravi prepared (Ravi shares a spreadsheet link in the chat).
[25:12] Ravi: (screen) First scenario: baseline hosted, no cache. Cost estimate: ~>$400k/mo. Scenario two: hosted with KV/prefix cache and batching — estimated $100–150k/mo. Scenario three: hybrid routing with 50% cheap model + batching + cache — estimated $40–60k/mo. Scenario four: Dedicated with reserved pools tuned to your peak — estimated $25–45k/mo depending on utilization. These are initial ballparks.

[26:10] Marcus: Those numbers make sense; we're trying to understand how realistic that dedicated low-end $25k is — what utilization assumptions?
[26:18] Ravi: It assumes 70–80% sustained GPU utilization and effective token reductions from cache + routing. If utilization is lower, per-token goes up. We'll include utilization sensitivity.

[26:40] Anika: Also want to avoid cold start quality regressions when spinning capacity.
[26:46] Ravi: We'll show warm pool strategies and keep a small warm buffer.

[27:05] Marcus: Any hidden network egress or storage costs we should watch for?
[27:10] Samantha: Network egress in hosted may be billed separately depending on region and traffic patterns. We'll call out egress and KV storage in the spreadsheet.

[27:30] Peter: For hosted, data encryption at rest — who holds keys?
[27:34] Samantha: By default Redwood manages keys for hosted but we support customer-managed keys in some region/configs. Dedicated and Private give more BYOK options.

[28:00] Ravi: We'll also include a 'break glass' fallback scenario: if Dedicated capacity is exhausted we route to hosted — costs spike but availability preserved.

[28:20] Marcus: That's promising. For the pilot budget question, can we structure a pilot with a fixed not-to-exceed cap?
[28:27] Samantha: We can structure the SOW with a not-to-exceed pilot budget and guardrails — we'll propose that in the pilot pricing.

[28:45] Anika: Ok, I have to hop to another meeting soon — quick recap of immediate asks from our side: we'll export token histogram and traffic sample; Peter will list compliance docs; we expect the Redwood price sheet.
[28:58] Samantha: Noted. We'll send docs by tomorrow EOD.

[29:12] Marcus: Any final questions?
[29:16] Peter: Nothing from me.
[29:18] Marcus: No. Good session.

[29:30] Samantha: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with links and action items.

[29:38] (call ends — automated note: remaining portion of meeting contained screen walkthrough of spreadsheet and a 20-minute technical Q&A between Ravi and Anika about sequence bucketing and caching TTLs; transcript truncated)
